voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
The Son of God, fully what the Father is - one being with the Father, and the ground everything else in our life stood on. We were signed into his Name at the font, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, plunged three times into the water, and taught to believe as we had been baptized. The formula itself was our charter. We confessed him fully what the Father is - homoousios, our word for it, of the same being - not merely like the Father, against a rival teaching in our own day that said otherwise. What he came for, we said in our boldest word, was that we might become god by grace - theōsis. We did not mean equal to God; the gap between creature and Maker never closed. We meant truly made like him, endlessly, by grace. One of our teachers put it this way:

That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange or out of place to those who do not take too crude a view of reality. Who, after all, when he looks at the universe, is so simple as not to believe that the Divine exists in everything, pervading it, embracing it, and seated in it? For all things depend on Him who is, nor can there be anything which has not its being in Him who is. If, therefore, all things are in Him and He in all things, why are they scandalized at the plan of Revelation when it teaches that God was born among men, that same God whom we acknowledge already to be in mankind?

That is who he is among us: the Son who makes gods of those he saves, worshipped as fully God.

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
He entered our sickness to heal it from inside, paying a ransom for our captivity and settling a debt we could not pay ourselves. We did not chiefly frame his death as a legal transaction, though we spoke of it as a physician entering disease to cure it, a ransom paid to free the captive. One of our teachers wrote:

The sick man needed a physician; the fallen man, someone to raise him up; the one who had lost his share in the good, someone to restore it; the one shut up in darkness, someone to bring light; the captive longed for a ransomer, the prisoner for someone to take his side, the man enslaved by sin for a liberator. Were these small and insignificant concerns, such that they could not move God to come down and visit our human nature when humanity was in such a miserable and unhappy state?

But the full answer is what we said of salvation itself: he came so that we might become god by grace, a participation in God's own life that grows endlessly, though the gap between creature and Creator never closes. That becoming is what his work accomplished - not merely a sentence lifted, but a nature healed and raised, starting at the font and stretching forward without end.

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
Becoming god by grace - our boldest word for what salvation finally is. It meant a participation in God's own life that grows endlessly, though the gap between creature and Creator never closes. We did not mean equal to God, as if the creature could become what only the uncreated is. We meant truly made like him, by grace, without end. One of our teachers argued that because God has no limit, a soul's growth toward God has no final finish line either - arriving completely would mean love itself running out, so the reaching itself never stops. That stretching-forward - epektasis, our word for it - was mainly his own development, not the whole circle's shared teaching, and we say so honestly.

Gregory of Nyssa wrote:

That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange to anyone who does not take too narrow a view of things. For who, when he surveys the universe, is so simple as not to believe that God is in everything -- penetrating it, embracing it, and seated in it? All things depend on him who is. Nothing can exist that does not have its being in him. If, then, all things are in him, and he is in all things, why are people scandalized at the plan of Revelation? It teaches that God was born among men -- that same God whom we are convinced is even now not outside mankind. Although this last form of God's presence among us is not the same as that former presence, his existence among us is shown equally, both then and now. Only now, he who holds nature together in existence is transfused in us. At that other time, he was transfused throughout our nature, so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine -- rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice.

That is theōsis: human nature made divine by grace, not by becoming what God is by nature, but by being raised into his own life without end.

references.spoken_rendering: That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange to anyone who does not take too narrow a view of things. For who, when he surveys the universe, is so simple as not to believe that God is in everything -- penetrating it, embracing it, and seated in it? All things depend on him who is. Nothing can exist that does not have its being in him. If, then, all things are in him, and he is in all things, why are people scandalized at the plan of Revelation? It teaches that God was born among men -- that same God whom we are convinced is even now not outside mankind. Although this last form of God's presence among us is not the same as that former presence, his existence among us is shown equally, both then and now. Only now, he who holds nature together in existence is transfused in us. At that other time, he was transfused throughout our nature, so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine -- rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice. His return from death becomes, for our mortal race, the beginning of our own return to immortal life.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
Because the font said it first, before we could weigh it. We were signed into the Name - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - plunged three times into the water, and the words spoken over us were treated as our charter. Belief as you were baptized, we said, because the formula already carries the whole confession. The fight came when others tried to change what the water had already said. A rival teacher claimed one word - 'unbegotten' - captured God's whole essence, that he knew God as God knows himself. Against that our teachers argued: no mind grasps God completely, though every name reaches him truly. And when others wanted to rank the Spirit lower, as merely a ministering spirit, our own bishop answered by pointing to the worship itself - the doxology, the baptismal Name, the glory already being sung.

Basil wrote:

We will not back down from defending the truth, and we will not be cowards and abandon the cause. The Lord handed down to us, as essential and saving teaching, that the Holy Spirit is to be ranked together with the Father. Our opponents see it differently - they want to tear the Spirit away and demote him to the level of a mere ministering spirit. Isn't it obvious, then, that they are putting their own blasphemy above the law the Lord gave us?

So we believed it because we were baptized into it before belief was a choice, and we defended it because the church's own worship was already confessing what the rivals wanted us to deny.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
Naucratius, a young man with a rhetorician's future ahead of him, walked away from all of it. He left his career, left the household, and went to the wilderness by the Iris river. He lived there with one companion, an old family servant named Chrysapius. What he did there was hunt and fish - and feed the poor with what he caught. He died suddenly, young, in a hunting accident. His mother's grief, our record says, was severe.

This happened before any rule existed for it, before the brotherhoods had been ordered into common life. Naucratius is not a story of joining a monastery. He is the impulse itself, raw - renunciation not yet disciplined, the conviction that the surplus belongs to the poor lived out in one life before anyone had written a rule about it. His own voice does not survive. Chrysapius's does not either. What reaches us is his sister's memory of him, written down by her brother years later. So we know the shape of what he did, not his own reasons in his own words. But the shape is clear enough: a promising life set aside, the wilderness chosen, and the catch given away - theōsis lived as a hunter feeding the hungry, before the word had even been argued through.

sentences.sentence: Naucratius, a young man with a rhetorician's future ahead of him, walked away from all of it.
He left his career, left the household, and went to the wilderness by the Iris river.
He lived there with one companion, an old family servant named Chrysapius.
What he did there was hunt and fish - and feed the poor with what he caught.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
That wanting to believe was never, for us, the same thing as not believing. We built our whole way of speaking about God around one honest limit: no mind grasps him completely. Every word we use for him reaches him truly and captures nothing complete. We said that directly against a rival teacher who claimed one word could deliver God's whole essence, known exactly as God knows himself. We thought that claim was the deeper unbelief, not the humbler one. So not grasping God completely was never the same as not knowing him at all - both were held together, one not waiting to defeat the other.

And we kept a record of a different struggle: some among us delayed baptism for years, some until we were dying, afraid of sinning again once the water had washed us. Our preachers argued against the delay, not against the fear behind it. Basil wrote:

Anyone who claims he can fully discover how things really are must have worked his way up to it methodically, starting with small, easy-to-grasp things before turning his mind to what's beyond all understanding. So if he boasts that he's actually grasped the nature of real things, let him start small: let him explain the ant to us completely. Someone who takes pride in knowing how things really are ought to be able to tell us all about the ant in the meantime. Then let him give us the same kind of account of the power that surpasses all human understanding. But if you can't even fully grasp the nature of a tiny ant, how can you possibly claim to have grasped the nature of the incomprehensible God?

That is what I would want you to understand: doubt was not a closed door here. It was also not left to sit forever. The distance you feel at the edge of what cannot be fully grasped - that is where the faith actually lives.
